subject: PSHE & RSE
source: National Curriculum / statutory RSHE guidance (Relationships Education, Health Education); PSHE Association programme of study themes; TGA RSHE Policy 2026-27 and TGA RECIPE Character Framework 2026-27 (Drive); existing TGA PSHE Y1-Y2 lesson style. Qur'an and hadith references limited to well-known authenticated sources and cited plainly.

lessons.title: Celebrating difference: respect for everyone
objectives: Explain that people are different and equally valuable
Show respect in words and actions

keywords.def: the variety of people and cultures in the world
an unfair fixed idea about a group of people
treating others with care and dignity
having the same value and rights
an unfair opinion formed without knowing the facts

starter: Name one way to be kind to a classmate.
Why should we avoid unkind nicknames?

teach.heading: We are all different
bullets: All are made by Allah and valuable
teach.note: Say bismillah. Ask pupils to share (right to pass) something that makes them unique, e.g. a language they speak, a food they like, a hobby. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day. Emphasise that we celebrate difference while holding to our values. Misconception: ‘different’ means ‘worse’. It does not.

teach.heading: A message from the Qur'an
bullets: Qur'an 49:13: people made into nations and tribes
So that we may know one another
The best of us is the most God-conscious
teach.note: Cite plainly Qur'an 49:13: Allah made humanity into peoples and tribes so that they may know one another, and the most honoured is the one with the most taqwa. Ask: ‘What does this teach about how we treat others?’ Take answers. Link to RECIPE Integrity and Eeman.

teach.heading: Stereotypes
bullets: A stereotype is a fixed idea about a group
‘All boys like football’ is a stereotype
teach.note: Ask pupils to think of a stereotype, such as ‘girls cannot be engineers’ or ‘old people cannot use technology’. Challenge each with a counter-example. Model how a stereotype can hurt. Remind pupils to use invented examples, not real classmates. Check understanding with thumbs up or down.

teach.heading: Showing respect
bullets: Do not make fun of differences
teach.note: Role-play a scenario where one pupil makes a comment about another's lunch or accent. Ask the class to suggest respectful responses. Connect to adab and the Equality Act: schools must protect people from unfair treatment because of characteristics such as race, religion, disability, sex and age. Keep wording simple.

practice: Sort into respectful or disrespectful: (a) listening to someone's idea (b) laughing at an accent (c) asking about their favourite food (d) copying someone's mistake to tease.
Challenge this stereotype: ‘Only adults can make a difference.’ Write a counter-example.
What could you say if someone mocks another person's lunch?
independent: Create a ‘We are all different’ poster with five ways people differ and one sentence about respect.
Write what Qur'an 49:13 teaches in your own words.
Role-play: respond kindly to an unkind comment.
exit: Define stereotype in your own words.
Give one way to show respect to someone different from you.
lessons.homework: Interview a family member about a time they felt included or excluded and write three sentences about what you learned.
lessons.send: SEND: use symbol cards and sentence starters. EAL: key vocabulary with images. Stretch: research a famous person who challenged a stereotype.

lessons.title: Bullying and cyberbullying: spotting it and stopping it
objectives: Describe different kinds of bullying, including online
Know how to respond and who to tell
Explain how to be an upstander safely

keywords.def: hurting someone on purpose, again and again
bullying that happens online or by phone
someone who sees bullying but does nothing
someone who supports a person being bullied
to tell a trusted adult or the platform

starter: Name two ways to be respectful.
Give one reason why people are valuable.

teach.heading: Kinds of bullying
teach.note: Say bismillah. Recap the difference between falling out and bullying from Year 3. Add that bullying can be hidden, such as exclusion. Ask: ‘Can bullying happen without anyone touching someone?’ Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day. Use invented scenarios only.

teach.heading: Why online is different
bullets: Messages can be seen by many
It can happen at any time
People may hide behind a screen
Words and images can stay online
teach.note: Explain that cyberbullying can follow someone home, since messages may arrive late at night. People may say things online they would not say face to face. Ask: ‘What can we do before pressing send?’ Teach the THINK check: is it True, Helpful, Inspiring, Necessary, Kind?

teach.heading: How it feels
bullets: Afraid to go to school or log in
teach.note: Be sensitive and supportive. Link to Islamic teaching: Qur'an 49:11 forbids mocking others. Remind pupils that the Prophet (peace be upon him) said a Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand people are safe (Bukhari and Muslim). Ask pupils to give advice to a friend who is being bullied.

teach.heading: What to do
bullets: Tell a trusted adult and keep telling
teach.note: Teach the response chain: Stop, Save, Block, Tell. Stress that adults want to hear and will help. Explain how to be an upstander safely: do not join in, support the person, report. Remind them of Childline (0800 1111) as a free confidential helpline.

practice: Is this cyberbullying? (a) A group chat where everyone mocks one child. (b) A friend disagrees politely about a game. (c) Someone shares an embarrassing photo without asking.
Use the THINK check on this message: ‘Nobody likes you, just leave.’
Write two sentences of advice to a child who is being bullied online.
independent: Create a ‘Stop, Save, Block, Tell’ guide with one sentence per step.
Write a script for an upstander message to support a friend who was left out of a group chat.
List three trusted adults and one helpline you could contact.
exit: Name two differences between face-to-face bullying and cyberbullying.
What are the four steps if you receive bullying messages?
lessons.homework: Make a family agreement on kind online behaviour and ask a parent or carer to sign it.
lessons.send: SEND: provide visual steps and scripts. EAL: pre-teach ‘retaliate’, ‘evidence’, ‘report’. Stretch: write advice for a school newsletter on being an upstander.

lessons.title: Feelings and worries: understanding and managing them
objectives: Name a range of feelings and where we feel them
Describe strategies for managing worry or anger
Link patience (sabr) and remembrance of Allah to wellbeing

keywords.def: a feeling such as happy, sad, angry or worried
a feeling of being anxious about something
peaceful and relaxed
patience and steadfastness
a plan or method that helps

starter: Name two ways to be a good upstander.
What are the four steps for cyberbullying?

teach.heading: Feelings are normal
bullets: All feelings are part of being human
Feelings can be big or small
It is okay to ask for help
teach.note: Say bismillah. Show an emotion wheel. Ask pupils to pick one word that matches how they feel (private choice). Normalise: even the Prophets experienced sadness; do not give details unless sure. Keep to: feelings are part of being human and we respond with good character. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Where do we feel it?
bullets: Notice the clues in your body
teach.note: Use a body outline. Pupils name signs of each feeling in the chat. This helps them notice feelings early. Misconception: ‘If I’m worried, something is wrong with me.’ Everyone worries.

teach.heading: Ways to feel calmer
bullets: Slow breathing: in for 4, out for 6
teach.note: Cite plainly: Qur'an 13:28 says that hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah. Practise a calm breathing exercise for one minute. Introduce the ‘worry box’ idea: write a worry and share it with a trusted adult. Encourage dua and dhikr alongside practical strategies and talking to others.

teach.heading: Patience and hope
bullets: Hard times do not last forever
Seek help from family and teachers
teach.note: Cite plainly: Qur'an 94:5-6, ‘with hardship comes ease’. Ask: ‘How did you cope the last time something felt difficult?’ Take volunteers. Link to RECIPE Resilience. Reassure pupils that asking for help is a strength. If a pupil appears very distressed, speak to the DSL.

practice: Match feeling to body clue: worried / angry / sad / excited → hot face / tight tummy / heavy chest / bouncy legs.
Try the breathing: in for 4, out for 6, three times. How do you feel?
Choose two strategies for when you feel angry. Why will they help?
independent: Make a ‘calm toolbox’ with five strategies that work for you.
Write a message to a friend who is worried about a test, using two strategies.
Draw or write about a time you felt proud after getting through something difficult.
exit: Name two ways to help yourself feel calm.
What does Qur'an 94:5-6 teach about difficulty?
lessons.homework: Practise one calming strategy each day this week and write a sentence about how it felt.
lessons.send: SEND: provide an emotion chart and picture strategies. EAL: translate feelings vocabulary and use gestures. Stretch: create a short guide for younger pupils on dealing with worry.

lessons.title: Privacy, secrets and asking for help
objectives: Tell the difference between safe surprises and unsafe secrets
Explain that our bodies and personal space are private
Name people and services who can help

keywords.def: the right to keep some things to yourself
something kept secret for a short time that makes people happy
something you are asked not to tell
a limit that protects you or others
a service you can contact for advice and support

starter: Name one way to feel calm.

teach.heading: Our bodies are private
bullets: Private parts are covered by underwear
Nobody should touch them or ask to see them
teach.note: Say bismillah. Use the NSPCC ‘PANTS’ rule as a framework: Privates are private; Always remember your body belongs to you; No means no; Talk about secrets that upset you; Speak up, someone can help. Use correct, simple language and keep a calm tone. Recap Year 1 ‘My body belongs to me’. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day. Remind that Islam teaches modesty and respect for privacy; adults must also respect children's privacy and safety.

teach.heading: Surprises or secrets?
bullets: Surprise: a happy secret, told soon
Unsafe secret: makes you worried or scared
Never keep a secret that hurts you
teach.note: Give invented examples: a surprise birthday gift (safe) versus someone saying, ‘Don’t tell anyone what happened.’ Ask pupils to give a thumbs up or down for safe or unsafe. Emphasise: if a secret makes you feel worried, tell. You will never be in trouble for telling.

teach.heading: Online privacy
bullets: Only talk to people you know
Tell an adult about pressure to send things
Adults must never ask for secrets
teach.note: Link to Year 3 online safety. Explain that anyone who asks you to keep online chats secret from your family should be reported. Teach the ‘trusted network’: five people or places to go to. Ask: ‘Who is on your hand?’ Draw a hand and write a trusted adult on each finger.

teach.heading: Getting help
bullets: Tell a trusted adult at school or home
teach.note: Share the helpline numbers and website in the follow-up message to parents. Practise a short script: ‘I need to tell you something that is worrying me.’ Reassure pupils. If any pupil discloses harm or fear, follow safeguarding procedures: listen, do not promise secrecy, tell the DSL the same day.

practice: Safe surprise or unsafe secret? (a) A party for your sister. (b) An adult asking you to hide a message from your parents. (c) A gift you hide until Eid. (d) A friend makes you promise not to tell about being hurt.
Draw your hand and name five people you could tell.
Practise saying ‘No, I don’t like that’ in a calm, firm voice.
independent: Write a short script of how you would tell a trusted adult about a worry.
Make a poster ‘Speak up, someone can help’ with the Childline number.
Write three sentences explaining the difference between a surprise and an unsafe secret.
exit: Give one example of a safe surprise and one of an unsafe secret.
Name two people or services you could tell.
lessons.homework: Tell a trusted adult at home what you learned about private parts and safe secrets, and agree on a family ‘safe word’ if they wish.
lessons.send: SEND: use picture sorting cards and a script card. EAL: use the PANTS visuals with simple key words. Stretch: write a letter to a younger child about speaking up.
